title: Global Refining Crunch to Keep Fuel Prices High Into 2027 as China's Oil Demand Falls 9%
subhead: Damaged Middle East and Russian refineries cannot be offset by spare capacity elsewhere, analysts warn, even as China's oil consumption posts its sharpest quarterly decline in years. The Iran war is tightening the product market even while headline crude stays high, and Baghdad quietly doubles Hormuz exports at steep discounts.

sections.heading: Refining Crunch Is the Real Story Behind High Fuel Prices
sections.body: The war's biggest market effect is no longer just crude supply — it is the loss of refining capacity. Analysts at Energy Trading Week Middle East in Dubai said damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia, plus insufficient capacity elsewhere, will keep global fuel prices elevated into next year and possibly 2027. 'Bapco is gone, the GTL Qatar is gone, Russian refineries are gone. It will take years to build them back,' Nikhil Agarwal of Globestar Energy told The National. Phillips 66's Brian Mandell put the damage in scale: 7 million barrels per day of refineries down in Asia and the Middle East, another 1.4 million bpd down in Russia. The IEA reported July refinery throughput of 80.9 million bpd — nearly 5 million bpd below a year earlier — with capacity elsewhere unable to offset product bottlenecks.
sections.whyItMatters: Crude may be in surplus, but the diesel and gasoline the world actually consumes are short. This reframes the war's cost: even a de-escalation in the Gulf would not quickly restore fuel supply, because refining assets take years to rebuild.

sections.heading: China's Oil Consumption Falls 9% as EVs and Electrified Trucking Bite
sections.body: China's oil consumption fell 9% year over year in the second quarter, according to an analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) cited by OilPrice.com. Electric vehicles displaced 36 million metric tons of oil in the first half of 2026, about one-third of the drop in Chinese demand; electric trucks drove the fastest shift, with alternative-fuel use in trucking up 90% year over year. Oil use also fell in construction, mining and chemicals. CREA says the decline cut China's CO2 emissions by 1% in the quarter — the first such reduction driven primarily by lower oil consumption — though power-sector emissions rose 3% on more coal-fired generation. Oil got more expensive after the Iran war disrupted Persian Gulf supply, accelerating the substitution.
sections.whyItMatters: China, the world's largest crude importer, is structurally reducing its oil appetite just as the Gulf war spikes prices. For producers, this 9% demand decline, not the war headlines, is the number that shapes the medium-term balance.

sections.heading: Russia's Oil Revenue Sinks as Urals Falls Back to $59
sections.body: Russia collected 326.2 billion rubles (about $3.76 billion) in net oil revenue in August, down 22% year over year and the lowest monthly total since February, OilPrice.com reported, citing Russian tax data. Urals, Russia's main export grade, averaged near $95 a barrel in the spring as the Iran war pushed buyers toward non-Gulf barrels — a windfall Moscow has now given back. Total oil and gas revenue fell 16% year over year. Moscow paid refiners more than 197 billion rubles in August to keep domestic fuel supplies, and refinery subsidies have reached almost 916 billion rubles since January as Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out processing capacity. Deputy PM Alexander Novak insists output will recover as refineries restart, but Rystad Energy cut its 2026 Russian crude output forecast to 8.95 million bpd, heading toward 8.6 million bpd in 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iran war's price rally briefly masked the strain on Russia's budget, but Ukrainian strikes on refineries and export terminals are now grinding down both output and revenue. Moscow's war-chest cushion is thinning at a time of heavy spending.

sections.heading: Iraq Quietly Doubles Hormuz Exports at Steep Discounts
sections.body: OPEC's second-largest producer more than doubled crude exports via the Strait of Hormuz in August to about 2.34 million bpd from 1.35 million bpd in July, Reuters reported, citing Iraqi officials and consistent with vessel-tracking from Vortexa and Kpler. Tehran granted permission to some tankers carrying Iraqi crude to transit the chokepoint, easing Baghdad's export bottleneck — though volumes still trail pre-war levels above 3.5 million bpd. Iraq offered deep discounts for Basrah loadings; China's refiners alone are estimated to have bought at least 16 million barrels of Basrah crude for September. 'Iraq has been giving heavy discounts... which has incentivised buyers to find shipping options to get the cargoes out,' Sparta Commodities' June Goh told Reuters.
sections.whyItMatters: Iraqi crude is re-entering the market at discounts that suit India and China's heavy-crude refiners, a partial, Iran-permitted normalization of Gulf flows. It shows trade rerouting around Iran's de facto chokepoint control is happening cargo by cargo, not all at once.

sections.heading: Japan's Biggest Tanker Operator Sees Hormuz Disruptions Dragging Into Next Year
sections.body: Mitsui OSK Lines, the world's largest tanker operator, now expects Hormuz shipping disruptions to continue well past the end of the year, its CEO Jotaro Tamura told Bloomberg. 'It's difficult to see operations resuming in any form by the end of the year,' Tamura said. The company had previously assumed navigation would gradually resume from October and normalize by January 2027, but this week's re-escalation — the first US-Iran strikes in more than a month — upended that. Traffic at the strait has slumped to a handful of observable transits per day, though dark crossings have smuggled more volumes out in recent weeks. Mitsui OSK does not plan to return to Hormuz until it sees guarantees and evidence of safely sustained passage.
sections.whyItMatters: The shipping industry's own risk assessment is the most concrete signal that a return to normal Gulf logistics is months away. This hardens the market view that tightness — and the refining crunch — are not short-term.

sections.heading: Shell Closes $16.5B ARC Resources Deal, Deepening Western Exposure to Montney
sections.body: Shell completed its $16.5 billion acquisition of Canada's ARC Resources, the company announced Wednesday. The deal adds around 370,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of liquids and gas production in the Montney basin across British Columbia and Alberta, at an enterprise value of roughly $16.5 billion including debt. Shell CEO Wael Sawan said it 'increases Shell's exposure to long-duration, low-cost liquids production' and targets compound production growth of around 4% through 2030. The equity consideration is about $13.9 billion, financed through $3.3 billion in cash and $10.6 billion in newly issued shares, with double-digit returns expected from 2027, per Anadolu Agency.
sections.whyItMatters: With Gulf and Russian barrels disrupted and refining tight, Western majors are consolidating secure North American supply. M&A is the quiet counterpart to the war-driven scramble — buying low-cost, geopolitically safe barrels rather than relying on chokepoint logistics.

sections.heading: Venezuela Deal Runs Into Creditor and Legitimacy Questions; US Uranium Output Triples but Imports Still Dominate
sections.body: Two transition-adjacent stories. First, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado backed a long-term US role in developing Venezuela's ~65 billion barrels of reserves but questioned acting President Delcy Rodríguez's authority to sign the 25-year deal, which covers 17 oilfields with a target of 1.5 million bpd, OilPrice.com reported. ConocoPhillips is owed roughly $10-12 billion from the 2007 nationalizations, and any new investment must negotiate that creditor queue. Separately, US uranium production tripled to 2.13 million pounds in the first half of 2026 — its highest since 2017 — yet that still covers only a fraction of the 46.9 million pounds US reactors purchase annually; Canada, Kazakhstan and Australia supplied 75% of deliveries, per EIA data cited by OilPrice.com.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington's Venezuela overture to add Western-controlled barrels faces the same legal and political fog that has blocked foreign capital for two decades. And on nuclear fuel, tripling a tiny base leaves the US dependent on imports — a supply-chain exposure the transition debate keeps circling back to.

bottomLine: Today the war's economic center of gravity shifted from crude supply to refined product. Middle East and Russian refinery losses — roughly 8.4 million bpd down combined per Phillips 66's count — mean fuel stays expensive well into 2027 even as China's oil demand posts a sharp 9% quarterly decline and Russia's revenue slides on sub-$60 Urals. Iraq doubling Hormuz exports at deep discounts shows trade is normalizing in pieces, but Japan's biggest carrier sees no full return before year-end. The structural takeaway isn't a chokepoint drama but a simple one: even if the Gulf de-escalates, the refinery capacity to turn crude into fuel won't be back for years.
sources: OilPrice.com, Anadolu Agency, CREA via OilPrice.com, Reuters via OilPrice.com, Bloomberg via OilPrice.com, The National via OilPrice.com, IEA, Rystad Energy, EIA, Vortexa, Kpler, Sparta Commodities
